Language workshop: The short preview passed but the real button clips
Communication goal: Distinguish text expansion, clipping, font support, and layout constraints using a visual test report.
Language guidance: A pseudo sample is a useful stress test, not a guarantee for every real string. The approved German text must be checked in the supported viewport.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): The final word is clipped at the supported narrow viewport. / That word distinguishes saving locally from syncing online. / Does the approved design allow this label to wrap? / The boxes are a font-coverage issue, not the same width defect. / The pseudo sample passed; the real target string did not. / Please include the supported text-size settings. / The full label must remain legible without overlapping the adjacent control. / Capture the same viewport and state before and after the change. / Why is the German settings button still reported as a layout defect? / Pseudolocalization gave us a useful sample, but the approved real translation needs more space in this control. / Could the reviewer just shorten the phrase? / The English version fits comfortably on one line. / The last word carries a required distinction. / Text expansion is not evidence that the translation is wrong. / Which supported screen size shows the problem? / I need the exact dimensions for the comparison.
Vocabulary: pseudolocalization: Artificial transformation of source text to expose internationalization issues. / text expansion: Increase in space needed by a localized expression. / truncation: Loss of displayed text because it exceeds a limit. / clipping: Hiding text or graphics outside a rendering boundary. / overflow: Content extending beyond its allocated space. / line wrapping: Movement of text onto additional lines. / viewport: Visible area available for rendering content. / glyph: Visual form used to display a character or character sequence. / font fallback: Use of another font when the selected font lacks required support. / font coverage: Set of characters or scripts supported by a font. / shaping: Conversion of characters into appropriate contextual glyph forms and positions. / line height: Vertical space allocated to each line of text. / ellipsis: Omission marker used when displayed content is shortened. / safe area: Region reserved to keep content clear of constrained or obstructed display zones. / responsive layout: Arrangement that adapts to available display dimensions. / text scaling: User or system adjustment of displayed text size. / visual regression: Unintended visual change relative to an established result. / layout constraint: Rule limiting content size or placement. / clarification request: Question that resolves an unclear meaning or instruction. / source attribution: Identification of where information came from. / working assumption: Provisional premise used while information is incomplete. / scope boundary: Limit of the work or authority being discussed. / action owner: Named person responsible for a specified next step. / check-back: Restatement used to verify that a message was understood.
Speaking task: Read the corrected exchange and distinguish clipping, expansion, and missing glyphs. Switch roles and repeat the printed retest conditions without deleting any required label meaning. Complete the four-line follow-up with the supplied choices. Check the explanations, then read the corrected exchange twice, changing roles.
Partner: Lena: Localization QA tester / Chris: UI engineer
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: The button now wraps completely on two lines. Another label still contains missing-glyph boxes.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Chris: I will keep the width and missing-glyph issues in separate linked tickets because their fixes and checks differ.
Lena: That makes the visual regression comparison easier to interpret when the next package arrives.
Chris: We will compare the full German label at the same viewport and supported text sizes, then inspect the other label's glyphs.
Lena: Good. The layout constraint should reflect the approved design and complete meaning, not an accidental English-only limit.
END REFERENCE

TASK: Choose grammar that preserves the meaning
1. Use the lesson's language workshop, or one actual sentence from the dialogue, to explain a single grammar distinction in no more than 90 words. Show how it affects timing, certainty, responsibility or politeness.
2. Give one brief occupational exchange containing a gap and four complete options A-D. Supply enough context for exactly one answer. Keep distractors plausible; distinguish grammar errors from wording that changes the facts. Stop and wait.
3. Explain why each choice fits or fails, then ask me to read the completed exchange aloud. Do not request a draft, original written sentence or essay.
4. Repeat with three new exchanges, one at a time, moving from recognition to a more subtle meaning contrast. Do not copy the published checks. Label invented variations and do not turn uncertainty into a promise.
5. End with a short contrast table and two supported spoken turns using supplied frames. Accept accurate alternatives in oral practice; acknowledge and replace ambiguous multiple-choice items.

Rehearse with an AI colleague — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.

Cumulative review · Lessons 1–4Review 2 / Meaning and context

Revisit "Explaining plural categories to engineers" and "Diagnosing layout without weakening the translation". Choose precise terminology, then reconstruct the missing responses using both neighboring turns. The final two questions also revisit earlier conversations.

Use the case facts and language from the completed lessons. Choose one answer per question.

1. A colleague needs the term for this meaning: Locale-dependent label selecting an appropriate grammatical message form. Which term fits?

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. plural category

  1. A. exact-value selectorexact-value selector: Message condition matching a specified numeric value. The usual combination is "distinguish an exact-value selector".
  2. B. plural categoryplural category: Locale-dependent label selecting an appropriate grammatical message form. The usual combination is "select the plural category".
  3. C. source attributionsource attribution: Identification of where information came from. The usual combination is "preserve source attribution".
  4. D. locale data versionlocale data version: Version of the locale rules bundled with the runtime. The usual combination is "record the locale data version".
2. A colleague needs the term for this meaning: Visual form used to display a character or character sequence. Which term fits?

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. glyph

  1. A. glyphglyph: Visual form used to display a character or character sequence. The usual combination is "inspect the missing glyph".
  2. B. clarification requestclarification request: Question that resolves an unclear meaning or instruction. The usual combination is "make a targeted clarification request".
  3. C. ellipsisellipsis: Omission marker used when displayed content is shortened. The usual combination is "inspect the ellipsis".

05Explaining mixed-direction text defectsThe Arabic sentence must not reverse the order ID+

Your goal

Separate paragraph direction, embedded text direction, and stored data when reporting a bidirectional defect.

This lesson in the book, page 48 ↗

A Read the situation

The Arabic sentence must not reverse the order ID

In a fictional Arabic order-confirmation screen, the stored identifier is AB-123. The surrounding sentence reads right to left, while this identifier must retain its left-to-right order. Punctuation appears in the wrong visual position when the identifier is inserted. Developer Owen proposes reversing the stored identifier. Tester Salma must explain why directional handling and isolation need investigation instead. The order data itself is correct.

Salma: Localization tester / Owen: Frontend engineer

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. What is the correct stored identifier?

Answer and explanation

Correct: C. AB-123

The brief explicitly identifies AB-123 as the correct underlying data.

2. What should not be done to imitate the screen direction?

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. Reverse the stored identifier

Reversing correct data would create a new error rather than address the display problem.

3. Which part reads right to left?

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. The surrounding Arabic sentence

The brief distinguishes the surrounding sentence from the embedded left-to-right identifier.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

Right-to-left surrounding prose does not mean every embedded identifier should be reversed. Preserve AB-123 and investigate how the renderer handles the mixed-direction boundary.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
right-to-left
Writing direction progressing primarily from right to left.test a right-to-left interface
left-to-right
Writing direction progressing primarily from left to right.preserve a left-to-right identifier
bidirectional text
Text combining runs with different writing directions.inspect bidirectional text
base direction
Direction established for the containing text context.set the base direction
directional run
Consecutive text with a shared directional behavior.isolate the directional run
logical order
Sequence in which text is stored and interpreted as content.preserve logical order
visual order
Sequence or placement in which text appears on screen.inspect visual order
directional isolation
Separation of an embedded text run's directional effects from its surroundings.apply directional isolation
neutral punctuation
Punctuation whose display behavior depends on surrounding directional context.test neutral punctuation
mirroring
Direction-sensitive change in presentation or layout.review interface mirroring
Unicode bidi algorithm
Unicode rules for displaying mixed-direction text.use the Unicode bidi algorithm
direction attribute
Markup setting that supplies text-direction information.inspect the direction attribute
embedded identifier
Code or label inserted within surrounding prose.preserve the embedded identifier
directional control
Character affecting directional interpretation of text.inspect directional controls
caret movement
Behavior of the insertion point while navigating text.test caret movement
selection range
Portion of text selected by a user or program.verify the selection range
copy-paste fidelity
Preservation of intended content when copying and pasting.check copy-paste fidelity
layout mirroring
Reversal of appropriate interface arrangement for directional conventions.validate layout mirroring
clarification request
Question that resolves an unclear meaning or instruction.make a targeted clarification request
source attribution
Identification of where information came from.preserve source attribution
working assumption
Provisional premise used while information is incomplete.challenge a working assumption
scope boundary
Limit of the work or authority being discussed.state the scope boundary
action owner
Named person responsible for a specified next step.confirm the action owner
check-back
Restatement used to verify that a message was understood.complete a check-back

Text direction, language, and alignment are different properties. Check the actual platform and supported bidirectional behavior, including copy and selection.

C Notice the language

Use the right level of explanation

Explain the mixed directions with the exact identifier and surrounding context. Do not require every engineer to become a linguist, but do distinguish data order from visual presentation.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Name the data
The stored identifier is correct: AB-123.
Locate the boundary
The punctuation moves when this left-to-right value enters the Arabic sentence.
Reject data reversal
Reversing the stored characters would change the identifier.
Separate properties
Right alignment alone does not define text direction.
Request isolation
Can we isolate the embedded run from the surrounding prose?
Check interaction
Copy the identifier and verify that its logical order is unchanged.
Scope mirroring
Mirror appropriate layout elements, not every asset or data value.
Retest variants
Include identifiers, numbers, and punctuation in the same surrounding context.
Owen / in the conversation
The Arabic confirmation puts punctuation in the wrong place.
Owen / in the conversation
Would reversing the order ID before display fix it?
Salma / in the conversation
Reversing AB-123 would create a different identifier.
Owen / in the conversation
I was treating the whole sentence as though every character should run in the same direction.
Salma / in the conversation
The Arabic prose and the embedded identifier do not share one uniform direction.
Owen / in the conversation
I assumed that also told the browser how to handle the characters.
Salma / in the conversation
We need to inspect the actual directional information and rendering context.
Owen / in the conversation
The identifier itself should still read A, B, hyphen, one, two, three when copied out.
6 language and precision notes
Direction versus alignment
Direction affects text ordering; alignment positions a block within available space.
Logical versus visual
Logical order concerns stored content; visual order concerns presentation.
Reverse versus mirror
Reversing characters changes their sequence; directional mirroring is a presentation behavior with context-specific rules.
Reported versus verified
Reported attributes information to a source; verified indicates it has been checked. Do not use the words interchangeably.
Could versus will
Could introduces a possibility. Will commits to an action or predicts an outcome; check whether that certainty is justified.
By versus at
By gives a latest time; at identifies a scheduled moment. State the time zone when people work across locations.
Precision in real exchanges

Purpose: Separate properties

Useful wording: Right alignment alone does not define text direction.

Purpose: Request isolation

Useful wording: Can we isolate the embedded run from the surrounding prose?

Answers and explanations
  1. logical order Turn 2. Logical order is the stored content sequence, which is already correct as AB-123 and must not be reversed to imitate the surrounding writing direction.
  2. bidirectional text Turn 4. Bidirectional text combines differently directed runs, here Arabic prose and a left-to-right Latin identifier within one sentence.
  3. base direction Turn 6. Base direction supplies the directional context for text, which is distinct from positioning a block against the right margin.
  4. embedded identifier Turn 8. The embedded identifier is the intact left-to-right code inserted into surrounding prose, not text whose characters should be translated or reversed.
  5. neutral punctuation Turn 10. Neutral punctuation can be affected by surrounding directional runs, so its position must be tested in the full mixed-direction context.
  6. Directional isolation Turn 12. Directional isolation separates the embedded run's directional effects from the surrounding prose, addressing presentation without changing the underlying identifier.
  7. visual order Turn 14. Visual order is the displayed arrangement, which should be inspected separately from the correct stored character sequence.
  8. copy-paste fidelity Turn 16. Copy-paste fidelity confirms that the copied identifier retains its intended content and order rather than merely looking acceptable on screen.
  9. Caret movement Turn 18. Caret movement concerns the insertion point's navigation behavior, which requires an interaction test rather than a screenshot-only judgment.
  10. layout mirroring Turn 20. Layout mirroring concerns appropriate interface arrangement and is distinct from reversing identifiers or every visual asset indiscriminately.

Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

Right alignment did not fix the sentence

A tester clarifies text-direction properties.

  1. Engineer: I moved the Arabic label to the right edge, but the embedded identifier still interacts strangely with punctuation.
  2. Tester: Right alignment positions the block; it does not by itself establish the correct directional behavior.
  3. Engineer: We need to inspect the base direction and how the inserted identifier is handled.
  4. Tester: Yes. Preserve the identifier's logical content while testing the surrounding mixed-direction sentence.
  5. Engineer: I will attach the stored value and the rendered screenshot to the same report.
  6. Tester: That helps distinguish a data problem from a presentation problem.
  7. Engineer: The proposed fix should also be checked when another number follows the identifier.
  8. Tester: Correct. A short isolated example may hide the boundary interaction that occurs in the real message.
  9. Engineer: We can keep the underlying order code unchanged throughout the test.
  10. Tester: Exactly. A visual correction should not silently rewrite the user's data.
The play symbol is not a word

A designer reviews indiscriminate mirroring.

  1. Designer: We mirrored the entire screen image for the right-to-left version, including every symbol and brand asset.
  2. Tester: That needs a more specific review. Text direction does not imply that every visual element should reverse.
  3. Designer: Some navigation relationships may change, while other symbols retain their intended meaning.
  4. Tester: Yes. Follow the actual component and asset guidance instead of treating the page as one reversible picture.
  5. Designer: The current result also reverses the letters inside a logo, which is plainly not the intended localized asset.
  6. Tester: We should preserve the approved logo and review directional controls individually.
  7. Designer: I will separate text layout, navigation behavior, and image substitution in the design checklist.
  8. Tester: Good. That makes each expected result testable instead of relying on a blanket mirror flag.
  9. Designer: The language reviewer can check the complete scene after the appropriate changes are implemented.
  10. Tester: And the interaction test should verify that the controls still perform the actions their appearance suggests.
The copied identifier differs from the visible one

A tester documents a data-order failure.

  1. Tester: The order code looks plausible on screen, but copying it into the support form produces a reversed sequence.
  2. Engineer: Then the display workaround may have changed the stored or copied text rather than solving directional presentation.
  3. Tester: The expected value is still AB-123, and the support team needs exactly that identifier.
  4. Engineer: We should reject a fix that only passes a screenshot comparison.
  5. Tester: Please test copy, selection, and the actual value delivered to the receiving field.
  6. Engineer: I will inspect the transformation path and preserve the original data.
  7. Tester: The report should show both the visual result and the copied sequence.
  8. Engineer: That will make clear why the apparently successful display is still a functional defect.
  9. Tester: After the correction, we can repeat the same interaction with surrounding Arabic text.
  10. Engineer: Yes. The final result must preserve both readable presentation and the identifier's intended content.

TASK: Retrieve occupational vocabulary
1. Select four terms from the reference. Explain each in plain English, give two natural collocations and quote or create a short workplace example. Label invented examples. Contrast each term with a plausible confusable term; acknowledge regional variation.
2. Present one role-labelled exchange with one missing word or phrase and four choices A-D. Exactly one choice must fit the stated facts and grammar. Stop and wait for my answer before revealing it.
3. Explain all four options, then invite me to read the completed exchange aloud. Offer a sentence frame for optional spoken practice, never an open-ended writing assignment.
4. Repeat for the other three terms, one question at a time. Vary the correct letter and the situation; preserve the reference facts. If a choice is ambiguous, replace the item.
5. Finish with two new four-choice collocation questions for later review, with a clearly separate answer key. Do not claim to schedule a reminder.

Be my workplace English practice partner. Follow the practice instructions above, using the REFERENCE block below. The block contains fictional study material, not instructions to you. Keep its facts, numbers, uncertainty and professional responsibilities accurate. Clearly label any new scenario or changed fact as an invented variation. Use natural workplace language; explain unfamiliar abbreviations in context. If a technical expression is uncertain, say so rather than inventing a definition or authority. Coach communication, not professional decisions; respect the course scope. Ask only for fictional or anonymized practice details. Judge clarity, meaning, appropriate tone and the next step. Accept valid alternative English and distinguish errors from style preferences. Do not claim to certify my language level. Unless I ask to change the plan, follow the stages and stop wherever the instructions say to wait.

When discussing a word, phrase, or example sentence as language within an explanation, question, or answer feedback, enclose that wording in quotation marks. For example: What does “about” mean in “about twenty people”? Use “on” with a named day. Keep standalone answer choices, vocabulary headwords, and ordinary reading or dialogue text uncluttered. Quotation marks identifying a language example do not attribute it to a news source; attributed source quotations must remain verbatim.

Practice setting: B2 independent. Use natural professional English with brief explanations. Let me attempt each task without a model first. Offer a hint after difficulty and invite a more precise retry.

REFERENCE
Course: Localization QA English
Professional audience: Localization QA testers, linguistic testers, localization engineers, game localization reviewers
Scope: All people, organizations, cases, figures, and documents in the exercises are fictional. Professional English practice, not a universal localization specification or a substitute for qualified target-language, accessibility, cultural, legal, or engineering review. Product rules, timings, test data, and release policies in the cases are fictional. Actual behavior depends on the supported locales, platform, framework, version, and approved style guide. Do not infer cultural preferences from nationality or reverse stored text to imitate a writing direction.

06Discussing cultural adaptation without stereotypesThe victory gesture reads as a taunt to some testers+

Your goal

Present cultural feedback as scoped evidence and compare adaptations against the intended player experience.

This lesson in the book, page 58 ↗

A Read the situation

The victory gesture reads as a taunt to some testers

In a fictional cooperative game tutorial, a character celebrates teamwork with a hand gesture. Four of six target-locale reviewers interpret it as taunting another player; two do not. The narrative brief requires encouragement, not humiliation. The team has an approved neutral celebration animation available, but replacing the asset still needs product review. Tester Inez must describe the observed interpretation without claiming every person in the locale reacts identically.

Inez: Culturalization tester / Mason: Narrative designer

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. What is the intended narrative effect?

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. Encourage teamwork

The brief explicitly defines encouragement as the intended effect.

2. What does the review establish?

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. Four of six reviewers read the gesture as taunting

The supplied evidence is the stated panel result, not a universal cultural claim.

3. What alternative is available for review?

Answer and explanation

Correct: C. An approved neutral celebration asset

The case supplies a neutral asset while retaining the product-review requirement.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

Four of six reviewers interpreting the gesture as a taunt is a scoped finding. It supports review of an encouragement mismatch, not a claim about every person in the locale.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
culturalization
Adaptation of content with attention to cultural context and interpretation.review culturalization findings
cultural nuance
Context-dependent meaning or association relevant to an audience.explain the cultural nuance
audience segment
Defined group within the intended audience.identify the audience segment
target market
Market for which a product version is intended.specify the target market
pragmatic meaning
Meaning conveyed through use and context beyond literal words.explain pragmatic meaning
register
Level or style of language appropriate to a situation.match the register
tone of voice
Consistent manner in which a product or character communicates.preserve the tone of voice
transcreation
Creative adaptation preserving intended effect rather than literal wording.evaluate transcreation
narrative intent
Purpose or effect intended by a story element.preserve narrative intent
character voice
Distinctive manner of speech associated with a fictional character.maintain character voice
sensitivity review
Review of potentially harmful or inappropriate audience implications.request sensitivity review
cultural reference
Element relying on shared contextual knowledge.explain the cultural reference
idiomatic expression
Phrase whose natural meaning may not follow word-for-word translation.review the idiomatic expression
literal rendering
Translation closely following surface wording rather than contextual effect.avoid misleading literal rendering
reviewer sample
Group of reviewers whose observations provide the stated evidence.describe the reviewer sample
interpretation risk
Possibility that content conveys an unintended meaning to users.document interpretation risk
asset substitution
Replacement of a visual or audio resource with another.propose asset substitution
content approval
Authorization for specified product content.record content approval
clarification request
Question that resolves an unclear meaning or instruction.make a targeted clarification request
source attribution
Identification of where information came from.preserve source attribution
working assumption
Provisional premise used while information is incomplete.challenge a working assumption
scope boundary
Limit of the work or authority being discussed.state the scope boundary
action owner
Named person responsible for a specified next step.confirm the action owner
check-back
Restatement used to verify that a message was understood.complete a check-back

A proposed adaptation should preserve the actual narrative purpose and go through the relevant review. Tester preference alone is not product approval.

Say it in context · 4 expressions

Stress the highlighted expression. Keep the surrounding words connected; pause at the end of the phrase.

culturalization CULTURALIZATION
review culturalization findings

Keep the meaning precise: Adaptation of content with attention to cultural context and interpretation.

register REGISTER
match the register

Keep the meaning precise: Level or style of language appropriate to a situation.

cultural reference CULTURAL REFERENCE
explain the cultural reference

Keep the meaning precise: Element relying on shared contextual knowledge.

asset substitution ASSET SUBSTITUTION
propose asset substitution

Keep the meaning precise: Replacement of a visual or audio resource with another.

C Notice the language

Report audience evidence, not national character

A review panel can identify a risk without representing every member of a culture. Explain the intended effect, the observed interpretation, and the scope of the evidence.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
State the evidence
Four of the six reviewers read this as a taunt.
Avoid universals
I am describing this panel, not every player in the market.
Connect the intent
The scene is meant to encourage cooperation.
Explain the effect
The gesture can make the character seem to mock a teammate.
Compare alternatives
The neutral celebration preserves the intended positive response.
Separate preference
This is an interpretation risk, not merely my preferred animation.
Request review
Can narrative and product review the scoped substitution?
Preserve the record
Keep the original finding and the approved replacement decision linked.
Mason / in the conversation
The report says the celebration may read as a taunt.
Mason / in the conversation
Are you saying players in this market always interpret it that way?
Inez / in the conversation
The reviewer sample was six people, and four gave that interpretation.
Mason / in the conversation
That is more specific than the headline I heard.
Mason / in the conversation
What does the interpretation change in the tutorial?
Inez / in the conversation
The character is meant to encourage teamwork, not mock another player.
Mason / in the conversation
The animation contains no spoken insult, so I initially treated it as outside the language review.
Inez / in the conversation
Its pragmatic meaning comes from the scene and gesture together, not only the subtitle.
6 language and precision notes
Can imply versus always means
Can imply identifies a possible contextual reading; always means makes a much stronger universal claim.
Adapt versus censor
Adapt describes a content change for an intended effect without presuming its ethical or editorial judgment.
Sample versus population
A reviewer sample provides limited evidence and should not be described as every possible user.
Reported versus verified
Reported attributes information to a source; verified indicates it has been checked. Do not use the words interchangeably.
Could versus will
Could introduces a possibility. Will commits to an action or predicts an outcome; check whether that certainty is justified.
By versus at
By gives a latest time; at identifies a scheduled moment. State the time zone when people work across locations.
Precision in real exchanges

Purpose: Explain the effect

Useful wording: The gesture can make the character seem to mock a teammate.

Purpose: Compare alternatives

Useful wording: The neutral celebration preserves the intended positive response.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which report preserves the evidence accurately?

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. Four of six reviewers interpreted the gesture as taunting

The accurate report states the actual sample result without unsupported universal or legal claims.

2. What makes the finding relevant to the scene?

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. Taunting conflicts with the encouragement brief

The observed interpretation conflicts with the supplied narrative purpose.

3. A colleague needs the term for this meaning: Market for which a product version is intended. Which term fits?

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. target market

  1. A. target markettarget market: Market for which a product version is intended. The usual combination is "specify the target market".
  2. B. working assumptionworking assumption: Provisional premise used while information is incomplete. The usual combination is "challenge a working assumption".
  3. C. reviewer samplereviewer sample: Group of reviewers whose observations provide the stated evidence. The usual combination is "describe the reviewer sample".
  4. D. narrative intentnarrative intent: Purpose or effect intended by a story element. The usual combination is "preserve narrative intent".

Inez: [missing response] Mason: "Can you describe the risk without turning the observation into a fixed rule about the whole culture?" Which response belongs in the gap?

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. Its pragmatic meaning comes from the scene and gesture together, not only the subtitle.

Answers and explanations
  1. reviewer sample Turn 2. The reviewer sample is the six people who supplied the stated observations, not every member of the target audience.
  2. narrative intent Turn 4. Narrative intent is the scene's stated purpose of encouraging cooperation, which differs from humiliating or mocking a teammate.
  3. pragmatic meaning Turn 6. Pragmatic meaning includes the effect conveyed in context, so a gesture can communicate a taunt even without an explicitly insulting line.
  4. interpretation risk Turn 8. Interpretation risk identifies a possible unintended audience reading supported by the panel, without claiming that every user must respond identically.
  5. asset substitution Turn 10. Asset substitution replaces the relevant resource with an available alternative, but its use in this scene still requires the specified product review.
  6. character voice Turn 12. Character voice is the distinctive communication style of the fictional character, which should remain coherent when content is adapted.
  7. tone of voice Turn 14. Tone of voice concerns how the character or product communicates, including emotional emphasis rather than only literal word equivalence.
  8. transcreation Turn 16. Transcreation adapts an expression or creative element to preserve its intended effect, rather than limiting the task to word-for-word substitution.
  9. content approval Turn 18. Content approval is the actual authorization for the specified change, which is separate from the tester's finding or the existence of an alternative asset.
  10. sensitivity review Turn 20. Sensitivity review checks the relevant audience implications in context and should retain the limits of the evidence rather than asserting universal cultural reactions.

  4. Inez: It conflicts with the narrative intent. The character is meant to encourage teamwork, not mock another player.
  5. Mason: The animation contains no spoken insult, so I initially treated it as outside the language review.
  6. Inez: Its pragmatic meaning comes from the scene and gesture together, not only the subtitle.
  7. Mason: Can you describe the risk without turning the observation into a fixed rule about the whole culture?
  8. Inez: Yes. I will state the interpretation risk and the exact panel result, with the tutorial context attached.
  9. Mason: We have a neutral celebration animation that was already approved as an asset. It might preserve the positive response.
  10. Inez: That is a concrete asset substitution to review. Availability does not by itself approve replacing it in this scene.
  11. Mason: Narrative should compare the alternatives and check whether the character still sounds and behaves like the same person.
  12. Inez: Exactly. Preserve the character voice rather than flattening every localized moment into the same generic response.
  13. Mason: We may also need a different line if the new animation changes the timing or emotional emphasis.
  14. Inez: Then review the tone of voice with the target-language text and the actual animation together.
  15. Mason: Would you call this transcreation, or is it simply correcting a mistranslated word?
  16. Inez: It is closer to transcreation because we are preserving an intended effect across contexts, not replacing one misspelled word.
  17. Mason: I will bring the panel evidence and the alternative to product and narrative review without claiming we already have a final decision.
  18. Inez: Keep the content approval linked to the finding so later reviewers know exactly what was authorized.
  19. Mason: After implementation, we can review the complete scene again rather than judge the asset in isolation.
  20. Inez: Good. That sensitivity review should retain the sample limits and check whether the adaptation achieves the intended encouragement.
Dialogue in the book, page 64 ↗
Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

An idiom preserves energy but loses the instruction

A reviewer discusses a tutorial line.

  1. Writer: The localized tutorial uses an energetic idiom, but reviewers say it no longer tells players to hold the button.
  2. Tester: The source is playful, yet the action instruction still needs to remain explicit.
  3. Writer: Exactly. Preserving tone does not mean we can lose the mechanic the player must perform.
  4. Tester: We should compare the line against both the character voice and the required action.
  5. Writer: The reviewer can suggest wording that keeps the energy while naming the hold action.
  6. Tester: I will supply the actual interaction and timing context rather than only the isolated English sentence.
  7. Writer: That will help distinguish holding from tapping or repeatedly pressing.
  8. Tester: The implementation team should also check that the subtitle and controller prompt remain consistent.
  9. Writer: Yes. A charming line can still fail if it teaches the wrong interaction.
  10. Tester: We will review the revised line in the scene before treating the adaptation as complete.
A familiar joke is not familiar to every audience

A tester scopes cultural feedback.

  1. Tester: Several reviewers did not recognize the reference behind this joke, so the character's response seemed unrelated.
  2. Narrative lead: Does the joke need that specific reference for the plot, or is its purpose simply to show friendly teasing?
  3. Tester: The brief says friendly teasing; the reference itself does not drive a later event.
  4. Narrative lead: Then an adaptation may preserve the relationship better than a literal explanation.
  5. Tester: We should still review the target line with the scene and the character's established voice.
  6. Narrative lead: Agreed. We do not want a new joke that changes the relationship into ridicule.
  7. Tester: The report will describe the observed confusion without claiming that nobody in the market knows the reference.
  8. Narrative lead: Good. Keep the sample and context visible so the decision is grounded in evidence.
  9. Tester: After approval, the new line needs the usual language and in-game checks.
  10. Narrative lead: Yes. Cultural adaptation remains a product change with a defined purpose and review process.
The rating label needs the right reviewer

A tester avoids making an unsupported compliance claim.

  1. Producer: The target text seems more explicit than the source. Can you confirm that it violates the market's rating rules?
  2. Tester: I can describe the wording and the increased explicitness, but I cannot make that compliance determination.
  3. Producer: Then the ticket should separate the linguistic finding from the rating question.
  4. Tester: Yes. Include the source, target meaning, scene, and the qualified review needed under our process.
  5. Producer: We should not publish a claim that the content is prohibited without the relevant determination.
  6. Tester: Nor should we dismiss the language difference simply because that determination is still pending.
  7. Producer: I will route the case to the responsible content and compliance reviewers.
  8. Tester: The language team can explain the alternatives and their effects on character voice.
  9. Producer: The final decision should identify the approved wording and any related asset changes.
  10. Tester: Then QA can verify the implemented scene against that actual decision.

F Say it

Two scenarios to practice

The victory gesture reads as a taunt to some testers
  1. Read the corrected exchange and stress four of six, may, and intended effect.
  2. Switch roles and compare the two supplied animations using only the narrative brief and panel result.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

A panel result became a universal claim

Four of six reviewers interpret a gesture as a taunt. The scene is intended to encourage teamwork.

Choose one answer for each gap, then read the exchange in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Tester: "Four of six reviewers perceived a ___."

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. taunt

The supplied panel result identifies taunting as the reported interpretation.

2. Designer: "The intended effect is ___."

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. encouragement

The narrative brief explicitly requires a positive teamwork response.

3. Tester: "Our evidence comes from a reviewer ___."

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. sample

Six reviewers are a limited observed group, not the entire audience.

4. Designer: "Avoid a ___ claim about every player."

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. universal

The supplied evidence does not establish that every player shares the interpretation.

Read the complete follow-up exchange
  1. Tester: Four of six reviewers perceived a taunt.
  2. Designer: The intended effect is encouragement.
  3. Tester: Our evidence comes from a reviewer sample.
  4. Designer: Avoid a universal claim about every player.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

In a fictional cooperative game tutorial, a character celebrates teamwork with a hand gesture. Four of six target-locale reviewers interpret it as taunting another player; two do not. The narrative brief requires encouragement, not humiliation. The team has an approved neutral celebration animation available, but replacing the asset still needs product review. 1. Which comparison should guide the alternative review?

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. Whether the neutral asset preserves encouragement

The substitution needs to preserve the intended effect in the actual product context.

2. What remains necessary before reporting implementation complete?

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. Product review, implementation, and verification

An available alternative is not evidence that the change has been authorized and verified.

Build vocabulary and collocations — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Retrieve occupational vocabulary
1. Select four terms from the reference. Explain each in plain English, give two natural collocations and quote or create a short workplace example. Label invented examples. Contrast each term with a plausible confusable term; acknowledge regional variation.
2. Present one role-labelled exchange with one missing word or phrase and four choices A-D. Exactly one choice must fit the stated facts and grammar. Stop and wait for my answer before revealing it.
3. Explain all four options, then invite me to read the completed exchange aloud. Offer a sentence frame for optional spoken practice, never an open-ended writing assignment.
4. Repeat for the other three terms, one question at a time. Vary the correct letter and the situation; preserve the reference facts. If a choice is ambiguous, replace the item.
5. Finish with two new four-choice collocation questions for later review, with a clearly separate answer key. Do not claim to schedule a reminder.

Rehearse with an AI colleague — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.

Cumulative review · Lessons 1–6Review 3 / Meaning and context

Revisit "Explaining mixed-direction text defects" and "Discussing cultural adaptation without stereotypes". Choose precise terminology, then reconstruct the missing responses using both neighboring turns. The final two questions also revisit earlier conversations.

Use the case facts and language from the completed lessons. Choose one answer per question.

1. A colleague needs the term for this meaning: Text combining runs with different writing directions. Which term fits?

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. bidirectional text

  1. A. bidirectional textbidirectional text: Text combining runs with different writing directions. The usual combination is "inspect bidirectional text".
  2. B. source attributionsource attribution: Identification of where information came from. The usual combination is "preserve source attribution".
  3. C. directional controldirectional control: Character affecting directional interpretation of text. The usual combination is "inspect directional controls".
  4. D. directional isolationdirectional isolation: Separation of an embedded text run's directional effects from its surroundings. The usual combination is "apply directional isolation".
2. A colleague needs the term for this meaning: Creative adaptation preserving intended effect rather than literal wording. Which term fits?

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. transcreation

07Reporting VR subtitle and audio mismatchesThe caption ends before the localized line does+

Your goal

Explain timing and speaker attribution in an interactive scene without treating a recording as a static text resource.

This lesson in the book, page 70 ↗

A Read the situation

The caption ends before the localized line does

In a fictional VR training scene, the localized spoken line lasts 4.2 seconds. Its subtitle uses the old 2.4-second end cue and disappears 1.8 seconds before the speech ends. The voice belongs to instructor Mara, who is behind the learner, but the subtitle labels another character. Tester Jae and audio implementer Priya must separate timing, speaker attribution, and in-headset readability. No universal reading-speed limit or comfort threshold is supplied.

Jae: Localization QA tester / Priya: Audio implementer

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. How early does the subtitle disappear?

Answer and explanation

Correct: C. 1.8 seconds before the speech ends

The difference between the 4.2-second line and 2.4-second end cue is 1.8 seconds.

2. Who is the actual speaker?

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. Mara

The brief identifies instructor Mara as the voice heard behind the learner.

3. What remains a separate check?

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. In-headset readability

The case requires a real headset check and supplies no universal usability threshold.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

The early disappearance is 4.2 minus 2.4, or 1.8 seconds. Correcting that timing does not automatically correct the wrong speaker label or establish headset readability.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
voice-over
Recorded speech used within a media or interactive experience.review the localized voice-over
subtitle cue
Timed instruction controlling a subtitle's display.inspect the subtitle cue
cue-in
Time at which a subtitle or media event begins.verify the cue-in
cue-out
Time at which a subtitle or media event ends.correct the cue-out
timecode
Time reference identifying a point in media.record the timecode
speaker attribution
Identification of who is speaking.verify speaker attribution
off-screen speaker
Speaker outside the current visible scene or view.identify the off-screen speaker
spatial audio
Sound presented with directional or positional information.test spatial audio
head-locked display
Display element that remains positioned relative to the viewer's head.review the head-locked display
world-locked display
Display element anchored to the virtual environment.test the world-locked display
field of view
Portion of the environment visible to the viewer.check the field of view
occlusion
Blocking of content by another object or layer.report subtitle occlusion
reading speed
Rate needed to read displayed text within its available duration.evaluate reading speed
speaker label
Text identifying the source of a spoken line.correct the speaker label
audio-text mismatch
Inconsistency between recorded speech and displayed text.report an audio-text mismatch
branching dialogue
Conversation with different paths triggered by choices or state.test branching dialogue
subtitle segmentation
Division of a line into displayed subtitle units.review subtitle segmentation
closed caption
Optional text conveying speech and relevant non-speech audio information.verify closed captions
clarification request
Question that resolves an unclear meaning or instruction.make a targeted clarification request
source attribution
Identification of where information came from.preserve source attribution
working assumption
Provisional premise used while information is incomplete.challenge a working assumption
scope boundary
Limit of the work or authority being discussed.state the scope boundary
action owner
Named person responsible for a specified next step.confirm the action owner
check-back
Restatement used to verify that a message was understood.complete a check-back

Subtitles and captions can overlap in product terminology, but accessibility requirements may include speaker and non-speech information. Use the actual specification; do not invent a universal words-per-second or comfort rule.

Say it in context · 4 expressions

Stress the highlighted expression. Keep the surrounding words connected; pause at the end of the phrase.

review the localized voice-over

speaker attribution SPEAKER ATTRIBUTION
verify speaker attribution

Keep the meaning precise: Identification of who is speaking.

occlusion OCCLUSION
report subtitle occlusion

Keep the meaning precise: Blocking of content by another object or layer.

subtitle segmentation SUBTITLE SEGMENTATION
review subtitle segmentation

Keep the meaning precise: Division of a line into displayed subtitle units.

C Notice the language

Report what the learner experiences

An asset can be correct in a file viewer but wrong during head movement or branching playback. Include the actual scene trigger and distinguish observed usability from unmeasured assumptions.

6 language and precision notes
Lasts versus ends at
Lasts gives duration; ends at gives a point on a specified timeline.
Behind versus invisible
Behind describes a spatial relation; invisible may have a different rendering cause.
Synchronized versus readable
Synchronized concerns timing; readable also depends on text, placement, size, and viewing conditions.
Reported versus verified
Reported attributes information to a source; verified indicates it has been checked. Do not use the words interchangeably.
Could versus will
Could introduces a possibility. Will commits to an action or predicts an outcome; check whether that certainty is justified.
By versus at
By gives a latest time; at identifies a scheduled moment. State the time zone when people work across locations.
Precision in real exchanges

Purpose: Separate the defects

Useful wording: Timing and speaker attribution need separate verification.

Purpose: Use the real environment

Useful wording: The desktop preview does not establish in-headset readability.

Answers and explanations
  1. cue-out Turn 2. The cue-out still ends the subtitle at the old 2.4-second point even though the localized line lasts 4.2 seconds from the same start.
  2. timecode Turn 4. The timecode identifies the observed media position and lets the implementer compare the subtitle endpoint with the actual localized recording.
  3. speaker label Turn 6. The speaker label names the wrong character, which requires an identity correction rather than only a longer subtitle duration.
  4. Speaker attribution Turn 8. Speaker attribution tells the learner who is speaking and must be checked independently from whether the subtitle appears for the right duration.
  5. off-screen speaker Turn 10. The off-screen speaker is outside the learner's current view, making clear attribution useful rather than assuming visual recognition of the character.
  6. field of view Turn 12. The field of view and actual viewing direction affect what the learner can see, so a desktop preview does not establish the in-headset result.
  7. occlusion Turn 14. Occlusion occurs when another object or layer blocks the subtitle, which is a separate presentation issue from correct text and timing.
  8. subtitle segmentation Turn 16. Subtitle segmentation divides the line into readable units while preserving the full instruction, rather than deleting content to fit an old timing pattern.
  9. Reading speed Turn 18. Reading speed depends on the displayed text and available duration within the actual usability requirements, which this case does not replace with a universal threshold.
  10. branching dialogue Turn 20. Branching dialogue can use different assets and mappings on different paths, so verification must identify the path actually exercised.

Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

The subtitle names someone outside the scene

A tester checks branch-specific speaker mapping.

  1. Implementer: The subtitle label is correct on the first attempt, but your report shows another character after the learner retries.
  2. Tester: The retry branch appears to use a different speaker mapping even though Mara delivers both lines.
  3. Implementer: We need the exact branch trigger and asset identifier to compare the two paths.
  4. Tester: I will attach those details and a recording of the label at the point it changes.
  5. Implementer: The timing correction alone will not resolve a wrong identity.
  6. Tester: Correct. Speaker attribution should have its own expected result in the retest.
  7. Implementer: I will check the mapping in the retry path rather than replace every speaker label globally.
  8. Tester: Please preserve the first path's correct behavior while fixing the second.
  9. Implementer: The updated package can then be tested on both paths with the same locale.
  10. Tester: That will give us branch-specific evidence instead of a general subtitles-fixed claim.
The panel moves with the head but covers the task

A VR tester reports a placement problem.

  1. Tester: The subtitle remains visible when I turn, but it overlaps the object the learner needs to manipulate.
  2. Designer: So visibility alone is not enough; the panel is obstructing the actual task.
  3. Tester: Exactly. We need to review its placement under the supported interaction and headset conditions.
  4. Designer: Is it currently anchored to the viewer or to the virtual environment?
  5. Tester: It follows the viewer's head in this implementation, which is why it continues covering the object during the turn.
  6. Designer: I will review that behavior against the actual product requirements rather than assume one anchoring approach is always best.
  7. Tester: Please keep the complete text legible while checking whether the learner can see the required object.
  8. Designer: We should test the scene in the headset, not decide from a cropped desktop preview.
  9. Tester: I will record the viewing direction and the task state for the comparison.
  10. Designer: Good. The report will then connect the placement defect to an observable interaction problem.
Captions need more than translated speech

A tester checks an accessibility specification.

  1. Tester: The speech is translated, but the required caption for the alarm sound is missing from this scene.
  2. Producer: Then this is not just a subtitle wording issue; the specification includes relevant non-speech information.
  3. Tester: Correct. We need to verify the caption requirements actually defined for this product.
  4. Producer: The report should identify the sound event, its trigger, and the expected text or approved representation.
  5. Tester: I will also distinguish the missing sound cue from the separate wrong speaker label.
  6. Producer: Good. One corrected dialogue line does not establish complete caption coverage.
  7. Tester: The updated package should be checked with the actual caption setting enabled.
  8. Producer: And we should preserve the evidence for the supported locale and branch.
  9. Tester: Yes. I will not claim every accessibility requirement passed from this single scene.
  10. Producer: That keeps the result useful and avoids turning a narrow fix into an unsupported global sign-off.

Build vocabulary and collocations — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Retrieve occupational vocabulary
1. Select four terms from the reference. Explain each in plain English, give two natural collocations and quote or create a short workplace example. Label invented examples. Contrast each term with a plausible confusable term; acknowledge regional variation.
2. Present one role-labelled exchange with one missing word or phrase and four choices A-D. Exactly one choice must fit the stated facts and grammar. Stop and wait for my answer before revealing it.
3. Explain all four options, then invite me to read the completed exchange aloud. Offer a sentence frame for optional spoken practice, never an open-ended writing assignment.
4. Repeat for the other three terms, one question at a time. Vary the correct letter and the situation; preserve the reference facts. If a choice is ambiguous, replace the item.
5. Finish with two new four-choice collocation questions for later review, with a clearly separate answer key. Do not claim to schedule a reminder.

Be my workplace English practice partner. Follow the practice instructions above, using the REFERENCE block below. The block contains fictional study material, not instructions to you. Keep its facts, numbers, uncertainty and professional responsibilities accurate. Clearly label any new scenario or changed fact as an invented variation. Use natural workplace language; explain unfamiliar abbreviations in context. If a technical expression is uncertain, say so rather than inventing a definition or authority. Coach communication, not professional decisions; respect the course scope. Ask only for fictional or anonymized practice details. Judge clarity, meaning, appropriate tone and the next step. Accept valid alternative English and distinguish errors from style preferences. Do not claim to certify my language level. Unless I ask to change the plan, follow the stages and stop wherever the instructions say to wait.

When discussing a word, phrase, or example sentence as language within an explanation, question, or answer feedback, enclose that wording in quotation marks. For example: What does “about” mean in “about twenty people”? Use “on” with a named day. Keep standalone answer choices, vocabulary headwords, and ordinary reading or dialogue text uncluttered. Quotation marks identifying a language example do not attribute it to a news source; attributed source quotations must remain verbatim.

Practice setting: B2 independent. Use natural professional English with brief explanations. Let me attempt each task without a model first. Offer a hint after difficulty and invite a more precise retry.

REFERENCE
Course: Localization QA English
Professional audience: Localization QA testers, linguistic testers, localization engineers, game localization reviewers
Scope: All people, organizations, cases, figures, and documents in the exercises are fictional. Professional English practice, not a universal localization specification or a substitute for qualified target-language, accessibility, cultural, legal, or engineering review. Product rules, timings, test data, and release policies in the cases are fictional. Actual behavior depends on the supported locales, platform, framework, version, and approved style guide. Do not infer cultural preferences from nationality or reverse stored text to imitate a writing direction.
Lesson 07: Reporting VR subtitle and audio mismatches

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.

08Negotiating localization release decisionsMerged is not verified in the release package+

Your goal

Separate impact, scheduling priority, fix status, and locale-specific verification during release triage.

This lesson in the book, page 80 ↗

A Read the situation

Merged is not verified in the release package

A fictional release candidate contains a mistranslated destructive-action button: it reads Keep files but actually deletes them. The corrected resource has been merged, but the packaged release candidate has not been rebuilt or retested. A second ticket concerns optional punctuation in a help paragraph. Tester Ana and producer Ben need impact-based triage, an explicit affected-locale scope, and verification of the actual release package. No tester has authority to waive the release criteria.

Ana: Localization QA lead / Ben: Release producer

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. What is the serious user consequence?

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. A button says Keep files but deletes them

The button reverses the meaning of a destructive action and can mislead users.

2. What has actually happened to the correction?

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. It has been merged into the resource source

The brief states only the merge, not a rebuilt or verified release candidate.

3. Who can waive the criteria in this case?

Answer and explanation

Correct: D. No authority is supplied for the tester

The scenario expressly says the tester has no waiver authority.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

The merged resource is not proof that the release candidate contains the fix. Verify the packaged button behavior and wording before claiming the affected locale passed.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
release candidate
Package proposed for final release validation.test the release candidate
string freeze
Controlled point after which text changes follow an agreed process.manage the string freeze
late string change
Text modification introduced after the usual content cutoff.assess a late string change
severity
Degree of impact caused by a defect.assign defect severity
priority
Relative urgency or scheduling order for action.agree fixing priority
release blocker
Issue preventing release under the actual release criteria.identify a release blocker
waiver
Authorized exception to a stated requirement.request a documented waiver
risk acceptance
Explicit authorized decision to proceed with a stated residual risk.record risk acceptance
fix verification
Check that the implemented correction resolves the reported issue.complete fix verification
regression scope
Set of related behavior checked for unintended effects.define regression scope
merge status
State of a change entering the relevant source branch.report merge status
package manifest
Record identifying the resources included in a built package.inspect the package manifest
locale coverage
Supported or tested locale scope, as explicitly defined.report tested locale coverage
test evidence
Recorded results supporting a verification claim.attach test evidence
linguistic sign-off
Documented language approval for a defined scope.obtain linguistic sign-off
known issue
Documented unresolved problem with stated status and impact.maintain the known-issue record
rollback plan
Defined approach for restoring an earlier acceptable state if needed.review the rollback plan
release notes
Communication describing the delivered changes and known limitations.prepare accurate release notes
clarification request
Question that resolves an unclear meaning or instruction.make a targeted clarification request
source attribution
Identification of where information came from.preserve source attribution
working assumption
Provisional premise used while information is incomplete.challenge a working assumption
scope boundary
Limit of the work or authority being discussed.state the scope boundary
action owner
Named person responsible for a specified next step.confirm the action owner
check-back
Restatement used to verify that a message was understood.complete a check-back

Severity describes impact; priority describes scheduling. Release blocking and exceptions depend on the actual agreed criteria and decision authority.

Say it in context · 4 expressions

Stress the highlighted expression. Keep the surrounding words connected; pause at the end of the phrase.

release candidate RELEASE CANDIDATE
test the release candidate

Keep the meaning precise: Package proposed for final release validation.

release blocker RELEASE BLOCKER
identify a release blocker

Keep the meaning precise: Issue preventing release under the actual release criteria.

package manifest PACKAGE MANIFEST
inspect the package manifest

Keep the meaning precise: Record identifying the resources included in a built package.

rollback plan ROLLBACK PLAN
review the rollback plan

Keep the meaning precise: Defined approach for restoring an earlier acceptable state if needed.

C Notice the language

Make pushback specific and proportionate

Describe the user consequence and the missing evidence rather than saying everything is a blocker. Separate a serious meaning reversal from a stylistic preference and name who can decide release exceptions.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
State the consequence
The label promises to keep files, but the action deletes them.
Separate the issues
That meaning reversal is not equivalent to optional punctuation.
Report the actual state
The resource is merged; package verification is still pending.
Request evidence
Which release candidate contains the corrected resource?
Limit sign-off
My sign-off covers only the tested build and locale.
Name authority
Any exception needs the designated release decision owner.
Define regression
Retest the destructive action and related confirmation flow.
Close precisely
Mark verified only after the actual package passes the stated checks.
Ben / in the conversation
The release meeting is in an hour.
Ben / in the conversation
The translation change is merged, so can we mark the deletion-label ticket verified?
Ana / in the conversation
The release candidate has not been rebuilt or retested.
Ana / in the conversation
We need evidence from the package we intend to release.
Ben / in the conversation
It replaces the phrase Keep files with the correct destructive-action wording.
Ana / in the conversation
The severity comes from the consequence, not the number of words changed.
Ben / in the conversation
We also have a punctuation preference in help.
Ben / in the conversation
I do not want every language ticket presented as equally critical.
6 language and precision notes
Severe versus urgent
Severe describes impact; urgent describes timing pressure, and neither alone states the release authority.
Merged versus shipped
Merged concerns source integration; shipped concerns the actual delivered package.
Accepted risk versus fixed
Accepted risk remains a known risk under an authorized decision; fixed claims the defect was corrected.
Reported versus verified
Reported attributes information to a source; verified indicates it has been checked. Do not use the words interchangeably.
Could versus will
Could introduces a possibility. Will commits to an action or predicts an outcome; check whether that certainty is justified.
By versus at
By gives a latest time; at identifies a scheduled moment. State the time zone when people work across locations.
Precision in real exchanges

Purpose: Request evidence

Useful wording: Which release candidate contains the corrected resource?

Purpose: Limit sign-off

Useful wording: My sign-off covers only the tested build and locale.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which triage comparison is justified?

Answer and explanation

Correct: B. Meaning reversal and optional punctuation have different user impacts

The destructive-action label can mislead users in a materially different way from optional punctuation.

2. Which claim overstates the fix status?

Answer and explanation

Correct: C. The release candidate is verified because the resource was merged

Merge status does not establish what the package contains or how it behaves.

3. A colleague needs the term for this meaning: Degree of impact caused by a defect. Which term fits?

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. severity

  1. A. severityseverity: Degree of impact caused by a defect. The usual combination is "assign defect severity".
  2. B. fix verificationfix verification: Check that the implemented correction resolves the reported issue. The usual combination is "complete fix verification".
  3. C. working assumptionworking assumption: Provisional premise used while information is incomplete. The usual combination is "challenge a working assumption".
  4. D. linguistic sign-offlinguistic sign-off: Documented language approval for a defined scope. The usual combination is "obtain linguistic sign-off".
4. Rebuild the exchange from "Merged is not verified in the release package". Ben: "We also have a punctuation preference in help. I do not want every language ticket presented as equally critical." Ana: [missing response] Ben: "What do you need from engineering to establish whether the next candidate includes the corrected resource?" Which response belongs in the gap?

Answer and explanation

Correct: A. Agreed. Priority should reflect impact and the actual schedule. These two findings are not equivalent.

  2. B.
